title: Land Revenue Systems and the Drain of Wealth

cards.b: Land revenue was the largest source of Company income. How it was fixed changed rural India and caused famines and debt. Naoroji and R. C. Dutt then showed how wealth left India. Few topics are asked as often.

• Permanent Settlement (Zamindari), 1793, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Varanasi: Cornwallis.
  • Ryotwari, 1820 (Thomas Munro, Madras), also Bombay: the cultivator is the owner.
  • Mahalwari, 1822 (Holt Mackenzie), 1833 (Bird): the village community pays together. North-West Provinces, Punjab.
About 19% of area was zamindari, 51% ryotwari and 30% mahalwari under British India.

The Company fixed the revenue permanently. Zamindars became owners and paid a fixed sum, about 10/11 of the rent collected. Failure meant the land was auctioned (the Sunset Law).

Effects: Company revenue became certain. Zamindars gained but many fell out and absentee landlords grew. Peasants had no protection of tenure until the Bengal Tenancy Act (1885). The land became a commodity and moneylending rose. Cornwallis hoped for improvement; little came.

Ryotwari: settlement directly with each cultivator, revised every 20 to 30 years. Rates were often high, around half the produce, which forced peasants into debt. Seen as “fairer” but in practice heavy.

Mahalwari: the village (mahal) headmen collected revenue. Revision every 30 years.

In all systems revenue was fixed in cash and in advance, whatever the harvest.

Cash demand pushed farmers to grow cotton, indigo, jute, opium and sugarcane. This is commercialisation of agriculture, driven by the market and often by the colonial state, not farmer prosperity. The Deccan Riots (1875) and the Indigo Revolt (1859 to 60) followed.

De-industrialisation: cheap Lancashire cloth and heavy duties on Indian goods (and free trade after 1813 and 1833) ruined handicrafts. Weavers moved to farming, raising pressure on land.

• Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901): drain was a “material and moral” loss.
  • R. C. Dutt, Economic History of India (1901 to 03).
  • Home Charges: pensions, interest, salaries and army costs paid in London.
The drain meant exports for which India got no imports in return. Naoroji put it at about £30 million a year (an estimate, disputed).

cards.h: How much did the drain cost?
cards.b: Nationalists such as Naoroji, Dutt, M. G. Ranade and R. P. Dutt saw impoverishment. Some economists, such as Morris D. Morris, argued that India was not that damaged and that railways and irrigation helped. Utsa Patnaik has recently estimated very large figures, which others dispute. The debate is about method, not that Home Charges existed.

Zamindari abolition was the first big land reform after 1947 (First Amendment and Ninth Schedule, 1951). Tenancy and land ceilings, and rural debt, still trace back to these systems. The drain argument shaped India’s early planning and its self-reliance stance. Famine memory shaped food security laws.

• “Examine the impact of British land revenue policy on Indian agriculture.” Structure: three systems, features, effects on peasants, commercialisation, famines.
  • “Explain the drain of wealth theory.” Define, give Naoroji and Dutt, Home Charges, evidence, criticism.
  • Prelims tip: Permanent Settlement areas, Munro and Ryotwari, and the year of each.
